extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students of mathematical analysis (calculus) learning computation of arc lengths, volumes and surface areas
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and formulae for computing volumes of solids with parallel bases and solids of revolution, surface areas of surfaces of revolution, and arc lengths (rectification) of plane and space curves, with worked examples (catenary, cycloid, paraboloid, torus, ellipsoids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of a solid with parallel bases (via sectional areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume of a solid bounded by two parallel bases and lateral faces obtained by joining corresponding points can be computed by summing the algebraic areas of triangular elements (projections) whose areas are polynomial functions of the perpendicular coordinate z; the total area S of a polygonal section is the algebraic sum of the triangular areas and thus a function of z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument shows that each triangular area is a polynomial (degree two) in z, so the area S(z) of a section is (in general) a quadratic function of z and the volume is obtained by integrating S(z) over the height. In the special case where the generating lines are all parallel to a given plane so coefficients vanish, S is linear in z and the mid-section area S_m = 1/2 (S_1 + S_2); the volume then reduces to the usual trapezoidal/prismatoid form (stated in text as V = A·(S_1 + S_2)/2 in that special case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariance of the section-based volume formula for ruled surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If one increases indefinitely the number n of generating straight lines forming the lateral faces, they approach a general ruled surface and the previously derived volume formula (from polygonal decompositions) remains valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The volume formula obtained by summing triangular contributions for finite n is preserved in the limit n → ∞; thus the same integration formula applies to slices (tranches) of any ruled surface between parallel planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of revolution by cross-sectional disks (disk method)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plane curve (meridian) rotated about an axis (Oz), the section perpendicular to the axis at height z is a circle of radius r(z); the volume of the solid of revolution is V = π ∫ r(z)^2 dz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the radius r as a function of z (given implicitly by the meridian equation). If coordinates are given parametrically x = x(t), z = z(t) one can substitute and integrate with respect to t. The derivation uses decomposition into thin slices perpendicular to the axis and the formula V = ∫ area(section) dz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume generated by rotating a closed plane region (contour integral form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a closed plane curve C (on one side of the axis of revolution) is rotated about the axis, the generated volume can be written as an integral taken along the curve: V = π ∮ x^2 dz (integral taken along C in the direction of the orientation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More practically, parametrize the closed curve by a parameter t (x = x(t), z = z(t), t from a to b traversing once) and compute V = π ∫ x(t)^2 z'(t) dt. This representation is especially convenient for closed meridians and when using parametrizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign/orientation convention when the generating curve crosses the axis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the generating curve crosses the axis of revolution, the contour integral taken along the closed curve represents the difference V_right − V_left of the two volumes generated by the portions of area on each side of the axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret dz as positive when the point on the curve ascends and negative when it descends; taking the integral over the oriented contour accumulates positive contributions for parts generating volume on one side and negative for the other. When computing volumes piecewise, evaluate volumes of the two parts separately and subtract as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus–Guldin theorem (Guldin's theorem) for volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: The volume generated by rotating a plane region A (homogeneous) about an axis in its plane that does not intersect it equals the area A multiplied by the length of the path described by its centroid: V = A · (circumference described by centroid) = A · 2πX, where X is centroid abscissa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the centroid coordinates given by contour integrals (formulas (5) and (6) in the text). If the region crosses the axis, the theorem gives the difference of the two generated volumes: V_1 − V_2 = A · 2πX (consistent with sign convention). The theorem also serves as a quick method to compute volumes like the torus: volume = (area of generating circle) × (circumference traveled by its center).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of arc length via polygonal approximations (rectification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of an arc AB is defined as the limit of the perimeters of inscribed polygonal lines AM_1M_2...M_nB as the mesh goes to zero; this limit exists and is independent of the way the partition is refined (assuming usual regularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text assumes that as each small arc tends to zero the ratio of chord to arc tends to 1; the rigorous derivation requires continuity and suitable differentiability hypotheses on parametrizing functions. This construction yields the integral expression for length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential element of arc (ds) for parametric curves
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve given by x = x(t), y = y(t), z = z(t) with derivatives continuous, the element of arc is ds = sqrt((dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2 + (dz/dt)^2) dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: consider the infinitesimal displacement MM' with coordinate increments d x, d y, d z; use that the infinitesimal arc equals its chord, so ds = √(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2). In plane curves this reduces correspondingly. Use this formula to integrate and obtain arc lengths; ensure the regularity hypotheses (continuity of derivatives) needed for the limit process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential of arc in polar coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: For a plane curve expressed in polar coordinates r = r(θ), the element of arc is ds = sqrt(dr^2 + r^2 dθ^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by expressing Cartesian differentials dx and dy in terms of dr and dθ: dx = cosθ dr − r sinθ dθ, dy = sinθ dr + r cosθ dθ, then compute ds = √(dr^2 + r^2 dθ^2). Use this for rectification and surface/area computations in polar form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface area of revolution between two parallels (lateral area)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area A of the surface obtained by revolving a meridian arc AB about an axis is A = 2π ∫ r ds, where r is the distance from the axis (radius) of the point of the meridian and ds is the element of arc along AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: approximate the meridian by a polygonal chain; each side generates a conical frustum whose lateral area ≈ (sum of circumferences)/2 × side_length, leading in the limit to A = 2π ∫ r ds. To compute in practice parametrize the meridian (e.g., x = x(t), z = z(t)), compute ds and r(t) and integrate. The formula is the analogue for surface area of the disk method for volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition into infinitesimal frustums/trunks (method of derivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both volume and surface area formulae are obtained by decomposing the solid/surface into infinitesimal elements (thin slices for volume, frustums/trunks of cones for surface area) and passing to the limit as element thickness tends to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For volume, sum areas of cross-sections S(z) and integrate in z; for surface area, sum lateral areas 2π r ds of infinitesimal frustums. This interpretation guides setting up integrals and choosing convenient parametrizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arc-length computation techniques and worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute arc lengths by choosing convenient parameters and algebraic/trigonometric substitutions or integration by parts; the text works examples including the catenary (chaînette), cycloid, parabola, and rectification in space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate: choose x as parameter for catenary and simplify radical to integrate; for cycloid use angle of rotation as parameter and reduce integrand via trig identities; for parabola use integration by parts. The text emphasizes adapting parametrization to simplify ds and checking constants so s=0 at chosen origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulas and approaches for specific solids (torus, ellipsoids, paraboloid)
rubrics_metrics.description: The textbook provides specific evaluations: e.g., torus volume equals area of generating circle times circumference described by center; surface areas of ellipsoids of revolution (prolate and oblate) are expressed via integrals requiring substitutions (leading to elliptic-type integrals); area of paraboloid zone computed with x as variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating such integrals, perform appropriate substitutions (trigonometric, hyperbolic, or elliptic substitutions) and check limiting cases (e.g., ellipsoid → sphere/hemisphere as parameters coincide). Use centroid/Pappus theorem for quick volume computations like the torus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parametric contour integration for closed curves (practical parametrization rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute integrals taken along a closed meridian curve C (for volume or centroid formulas), express x and z as functions of a parameter t so that as t varies from a to b the point makes one complete circuit in the chosen orientation; then replace line integrals by integrals in t (e.g., V = π ∫ x(t)^2 z'(t) dt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the parameter so the orientation matches the positive (arrow) direction used in the contour integrals; when the curve crosses the axis, split into arcs and treat separately. This prescription simplifies computation and avoids sign mistakes.
